newsitem.title: UK: Evidence grows of BSE in humans, relatives told.
newsitem.headline: Evidence grows of BSE in humans, relatives told.

text.p: Evidence is growing that people can develop the human form of mad cow disease from eating infected beef, a top researcher said on Thursday.

Relatives of people who have died from Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (CJD) met scientists who have been tracking the deadly brain illness for the first time on Thursday, one year after the link was first identified.

"Since last March evidence has strengthened that there is a causal link between BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy or mad cow disease) and CJD," said Peter Smith, an adviser to Britain's CJD Surveillance Unit and a member of the government's Spongiform Encephalopathy Advisory Committee (SEAC). The relatives, clearly angry, said this was the first time they had heard such evidence, although it has been published in the scientific press and reported by newspapers and television.
"Why has it taken one year to the day to use the term 'causal link?'" demanded Gerard Callaghan, whose brother Maurice died of a new variant of CJD last year.

Until last year, the British government said there was no evidence people could get sick from eating beef infected with BSE. But then a new variant of CJD, normally a deadly but extremely rare brain-wasting disease, was identified.
It affected people under 40 while CJD, because of its long incubation period, normally kills the elderly. It also showed distinctive patterns of brain damage.

Smith noted that while 14 probable and definite cases of the new variant had been identified in Britain -- the only country substantially affected by BSE -- only one had been seen outside. That was in France, which used to import British beef before the European Union banned its export last year.
Scientists have also noted that the molecular patterns of BSE when injected into test animals are almost identical to the molecular patterns of the new CJD variant.

Smith said no one yet knew how many people would get the new variant of CJD, as its incubation period was not known and it was not clear how much infected beef someone would need to have eaten to get sick.

Experts do not know how much infected beef got into the food supply before the government introduced bans on using parts of animals known to harbour the mutated proteins that are believed to pass on BSE.
"The next few years will prove crucial to gauge the size of any potential epidemic," Smith said.
